title: Check If a String Is a Valid Sequence from Root to Leaves Path in a Binary Tree
statement:
You get the `root` of a binary tree whose nodes each hold a digit from `0` to `9`, and an integer array `arr`. Every path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf (a node with no children) reads off a sequence of node values.

Return `true` if `arr` is exactly one of those root-to-leaf sequences (same length and the same values in the same order), and `false` otherwise. A path that stops at a node that still has a child does not count, and an empty tree has no paths.
notes:
## Intuition

We could list every root-to-leaf path and compare each one with `arr`, but that copies paths over and over. Instead, walk down the tree and `arr` together: at depth `index` the node must hold `arr[index]`. Any mismatch kills that branch at once, so only branches that still agree with `arr` are explored.

The answer is `true` only when the walk reaches a **leaf** exactly at the last position of `arr`. Running out of tree early or running out of `arr` early both mean "no".

## Approach

1. Define `dfs(node, index)`: can the path from `node` downward match `arr[index..]` and end at a leaf?
2. If `node` is missing or `index` is past the end of `arr`, return `false`.
3. If `node.val` differs from `arr[index]`, return `false`.
4. If `node` is a leaf, succeed only when `index` is the last position of `arr`.
5. Otherwise try the left child, then the right child, with `index + 1`; either one succeeding is enough.
6. Return `dfs(root, 0)`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree `[0,1,0,0,1,0,null,null,1,0,0]` and `arr = [0,1,0,1]`:

- Root `0` matches `arr[0]` and has children, so go left.
- Left child `1` matches `arr[1]`; go left to its child `0`, which matches `arr[2]`.
- That `0` has only a right child `1`; the left call returns `false`, the right child matches `arr[3]`, is a leaf, and `3` is the last index, so it returns `true`.

The `||` stops there and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(min(N, branches agreeing with `arr`)): each node is visited at most once, and mismatching branches are cut immediately.
- Space: O(H) for the recursion, where H is the tree height (bounded by `arr.length`).

## Pitfalls

- Matching all of `arr` at a node that still has children is **not** a valid path (Example 3).
- Do not stop after the left subtree fails; the matching leaf may be on the right.
- Check `index === arr.length` before reading `arr[index]`, otherwise a deeper tree compares against `undefined`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dfs(node, index)` | whether the path from `node` can finish matching `arr` from `index` |
| `node` | the tree node being compared |
| `index` | position in `arr` that `node` must match (its depth) |
| `isLeaf` | `node` has no children, so the path must end here |

narration.2: dfs asks whether the path from node can match arr from index onward and end at a leaf.
narration.3: No node here, or arr already fully used while the tree goes on: this branch cannot match.
narration.6: The node's digit must equal the value at the same depth in arr.
narration.7: A mismatch cuts off this whole subtree.
narration.9: A leaf has no children, so any path through it ends here.
narration.10: At a leaf the path is complete...
narration.11: ...so it matches only if this was also the last value of arr.
narration.13: Not a leaf: try the left subtree first, then the right one if the left fails.
narration.16: Start the walk at the root with the first value of arr.
